text: The Museum of Bad Art (MOBA) is a privately owned museum founded in 1993 with the stated aim of "celebrating the labor of artists whose work would be displayed and appreciated in no other forum." Originally located in Dedham, Massachusetts, it is now based in Boston, Massachusetts. Its permanent collection includes over 700 pieces of "art too bad to be ignored," with 25 to 35 on public display at any given time. The museum was established after antique dealer Scott Wilson showed a painting found in the trash to his friend Jerry Reilly, who suggested starting a collection. Within a year, receptions held in Reilly’s home attracted so many attendees that the collection required its own space, leading to the first exhibition in March 1994. The museum initially operated in the basement of the Dedham Community Theatre, a building described as "ramshackle," and had no fixed hours, being open only when the theater upstairs was open. The art was displayed "just outside the men's room," where the constant flushing of toilets was said to maintain uniform humidity. MOBA's co-founders, Jerry Reilly and Marie Jackson, hosted a reception titled "The Opening of the Museum of Bad Art" in their basement, and the museum later expanded to include a second gallery at the Somerville Theatre in 2008 and a third in the offices of the Brookline Interactive Group in 2010. The Dedham location closed in 2012, the Somerville location in 2019, and all locations ceased operations after the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, reopening in September 2022 at the Dorchester Brewing Company’s tap room in Boston. MOBA accepts original works with serious intent that contain significant flaws but are not boring or deliberate kitsch; curators are not interested in commercial art, children’s art, paint-by-numbers, or factory-produced items. Works must be compelling despite their flaws, and the museum emphasizes sincerity over technical skill. The collection includes pieces like Lucy in the Field with Flowers, acquired from trash in Boston, which remains a favorite due to its powerful and enigmatic imagery, and Sunday on the Pot with George, a technically proficient painting that has been described as "iconic" and "100 percent guaranteed to make you burst out laughing." The museum features rotating exhibitions, such as "Freaks of Nature" in 2003, "Hackneyed Portraits" in 2006, and "Nature Abhors a Vacuum and All Other Housework," which continues on the museum’s website. MOBA has been featured in international media, inspired other collections worldwide, and has received criticism for being anti-art, though its founders argue it celebrates artistic sincerity and the right to fail. The museum offers detailed, tongue-in-cheek captions for each piece, primarily written by Marie Jackson and later by Michael Frank and Louise Reilly Sacco. Many works are donated, often by artists themselves, or sourced from yard sales, thrift stores, or the Trash Collectors Union; occasionally, pieces are purchased, with a historical policy of spending no more than $6.50, though this has been exceeded for exceptional works. Pieces not accepted are included in a "Rejection Collection" sold at auction, with proceeds sometimes going to the Salvation Army. MOBA has faced thefts, including the disappearance of Eileen by R. Angelo Le in 1996 and the removal of Rebecca Harris' Self Portrait as a Drainpipe in 2004, both of which generated media attention and led to the installation of a fake security camera. The museum has also conducted fundraisers, such as selling Studies in Digestion on eBay for $10,000 with a $152.53 final sale to support the Rose Art Museum at Brandeis University. MOBA maintains that its mission is not to mock artists but to honor their effort and intent, and it has been recognized as a tribute to artistic sincerity, with visitors and students noting its value in demonstrating that pure intent is valid.

"Sunday on the Pot with George" (acrylic on canvas by John Gedraitis; donated by Jim Schulman) has been called "iconic" by Bella English of The Boston Globe, who notes it is "100 percent guaranteed to make you burst out laughing." Wilson highlights George as a technically well-executed piece featuring a subject rarely rendered in paint. The painting depicts a portly man in "Y-front" underwear sitting on a chamber pot, rendered in pointillist impressionism reminiscent of Georges Seurat. One critic speculates the pointillist style may have come from "watching too much TV." Author Amy Levin suggests the work is a pastiche of Seurat's painting A Sunday Afternoon on the Island of La Grande Jatte. The Annals of Improbable Research have tentatively identified the subject as John Ashcroft, former United States Attorney General. A visitor at the Dedham Community Theatre basement reported that the sound of someone peeing into a toilet while viewing the painting brought it to life, leading them to weep upon the flush. MOBA's caption questions whether the swirling steam can alleviate George's corporate burdens, noting the meticulous detail in elements like the towel's stitching, in contrast to the neglect of the subject's feet. In contrast to George's pointillist style, MOBA features a "fine example of labor-intensive pointlessism" in Mari Newman's Bone-Juggling Dog in Hula Skirt (tempera and acrylic on canvas; donated by the artist), described by MOBA staff as a puzzling image of a dog juggling bones while wearing a hula skirt. Newman, a Minneapolis-based artist, created the piece after buying used canvases as a student and being inspired by a cartoon of a dachshund; she added a hula skirt from a magazine and colored dog bones from a pet store, later writing that she almost threw it out until hearing of MOBA, and now wishes she had saved all her rejected work. Travel writer Cash Peters identifies six common traits in MOBA artworks: inability to render hands or feet, skies painted in non-blue colors, flora without botanical accuracy, fauna too small to identify, repeated attempts at noses creating a three-dimensional effect, and the use of mixed media such as feathers, glitter, or hair; he also notes that artists often include monkeys or poodles to save the work, believing it may be salvaged. Since late 2008, MOBA has allowed the public to title and caption works, with curatorial staff stating that mere interpretation is insufficient—works must be "interpretated." The "Guest Interpretator's Collection" invites visitor input, with a contest selecting the best analysis, which is then added to the collection. A Boston University professor remarked that MOBA's location and collection suggest a commitment to the abject and marginalized cultural effects, adding that he needed to pick up toilet bowl cleaner on his way home. MOBA has been mentioned in hundreds of international publications and Boston-area travel guides, inspiring similar collections in Australia, Ohio, and Seattle. Commedia Beauregard, a theatre company focused on translation, created "Master Works: The MOBA Plays" in January and February 2009 in Minneapolis, based on artworks including Mana Lisa, Invasion of the Office Zombies, My Left Foot, Bone-Juggling Dog in Hula Skirt, Gina's Demons, and Lulli, Fowl and Gravestone; the plays were later performed in March and April 2011 in Chicago, using three original plays and translating three new paintings. Visitors can sign a guest book; one Canadian visitor described the collection as "disturbing yet can't look away...just like a hideous car accident," while another noted, "Her nipples follow you around the room. Creepy!" Some responses to MOBA reflect broader societal attitudes toward art, with works described as "unintentionally hilarious," similar to the films of Ed Wood, and visitors and staff often laughing out loud—unlike at institutions like the Getty Museum, where such reactions would be considered inappropriate. In a 2006 panel on art and beauty, Louise Reilly Sacco noted that MOBA helps high school students laugh, point, and form their own opinions, freeing them from intimidation at the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston (MFA), and suggesting that extreme ugliness is more impactful than extreme beauty, forcing deeper reflection on what is wrong or misplaced, and connecting this judgment to intolerance for physical imperfections in people. Harvard professor Jason Kaufman identifies MOBA as part of a social trend he calls "annoyism," where media promotes deliberately bad art mixed with cleverness; he sees MOBA's strength in undermining aesthetic standards from multiple angles. Amy Levin views MOBA as a parody of art institutions, mocking museums as authorities on what constitutes good art through its commentary, newsletter, website, and publications. A director of the Ellipse Arts Center in Arlington, Virginia, who hosted a traveling MOBA exhibition, was surprised by the visitors' exuberant laughter, noting that no one had ever responded to art this way at her gallery and observing, "If I didn't have a sign on the door, people might not think it's so bad. Who's to say what's bad and what's good?" Deborah Solomon of The New York Times Magazine argues MOBA's success reflects a modern art trend where art appreciation has become more esoteric and inaccessible, with the public perceiving museums as intimidating places ruled by experts; she notes that bad art is in vogue as a rejection of earlier anti-sentimentalism toward artists like Norman Rockwell or Gustave Moreau. Garen Daly, a MOBA fan on Boston-area art councils, stated in 1995 that art openings can be "pretty damn stuffy." MOBA offers a different kind of experience, providing patrons with Kool-Aid, Fluffernutters, and cheese puffs instead of wine and cheese. MOBA artworks have been used in academic studies as a benchmark for low-quality art. One study in Perspectives on Psychological Science showed that participants rated MoMA art as higher quality, but conscious reasoning did not result in more accurate or consistent ratings; quick "gut" judgments were more consistent and equally accurate, with no significant difference in how MOBA art was perceived. Another study in the British Journal of Psychology tested balance in artwork composition, showing that participants could identify original balance in both traditional masterworks and MOBA pieces, concluding that balance alone does not define higher quality art and that participants saw original works as more balanced than altered versions, without finding traditional art significantly better composed than MOBA works.
